passage: When I joined the accounts office in Ludhiana, the first thing I noticed was the ledgers. Nandini ma'am, who had run the office for thirty years, still wrote every entry by hand and then typed it again. In my second week I made a slide deck about accounting software and presented it. She listened politely and said, "We'll see." Nothing changed. Later, over chai, she told me about the year the old computer crashed, a month of records vanished, and she was blamed. That's when I understood: it wasn't stubbornness, it was fear. So I stopped pushing. I asked, "Could we try the software for just one client, and keep your ledger alongside?" She agreed. Three months later she moved two more clients herself. "Gurleen, you're our careful one," she says now.

qa.q: How long had Nandini ma'am run the office?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel on hearing about the crash?
qa.a: Gurleen felt understanding and new respect, seeing that the resistance came from fear of losing records again, not stubbornness.

qa.q: Why did the one-client pilot work when the slide deck didn't?
qa.a: It respected her fear by keeping the ledger alongside, so she could see the software work safely before trusting it.

qa.q: What might Nandini ma'am have felt during the slide deck presentation?
qa.a: She may have felt pressured and anxious, remembering the crash and the blame, which is why she only said "We'll see."

grounding: A young professional recalls that pushing an elder colleague to change failed, while respecting her fear and offering a small pilot worked.

passage:
Headteacher's note, staff room, end of term
I want to record how Charu, our youngest teacher, handled the lunch-time change. For years the senior staff have eaten at 1 p.m. in the staff room while the children eat without a teacher. Last year, when a new teacher pushed hard to change it, Pooja ma'am and two others refused, and the staff room went cold for weeks. Charu noticed something different: Pooja ma'am wasn't against the children; she was afraid of losing the one quiet half hour in her day. So Charu asked for a small pilot: two teachers eat with the children on Fridays only, and the staff room lunch stays for everyone else. Pooja ma'am joined on the third Friday, on her own. We will review the pilot in January.

qa.q: When do two teachers eat with the children in the pilot?
qa.a: On Fridays only.

qa.q: Why did Charu ask for only a small pilot?
qa.a: Charu felt respect for Pooja ma'am's fear of losing her only quiet half hour, and wanted to avoid the coldness that pushing had caused last year.

qa.q: Why did Charu's pilot work better than last year's push?
qa.a: It kept the staff room lunch for everyone else, protecting what Pooja ma'am feared losing, so she could try it in her own time.

qa.q: How might Pooja ma'am have felt joining on the third Friday?
qa.a: She likely felt respected and safe enough to try, since nobody forced her and her quiet lunch was still there.

grounding: A headteacher records a young teacher who saw the fear behind senior staff resisting a change and proposed a small pilot instead of pushing.

passage:
Saturday night
Big lesson today. For months Preeti and I have been telling Dadi to move her bed downstairs because the stairs are steep, and every time she says, "I've slept in that room for fifty years." Today Preeti pushed hard again and Dadi cried. I've never seen her cry.
After, I sat with her. She said downstairs means she's "an old woman now," and that Dadaji's photos are in that room. It wasn't the stairs. It was losing herself.
So I tried something smaller. "Just on the hot nights, Dadi, when the fan upstairs is useless? We'll bring Dadaji's photo down too." She thought about it and said, "Only on hot nights."
Tomorrow is forty degrees. We'll see.
Anjali

qa.q: How long has Dadi slept in that room?
qa.a: Fifty years.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel after seeing Dadi cry?
qa.a: Anjali felt shaken and sad, and understood that Dadi's resistance came from fear of losing herself, not from the stairs.

qa.q: Why is "just on the hot nights" a wise step?
qa.a: It is a small pilot that respects Dadi's fear, keeps Dadaji's photo with her, and lets her try the change without giving up her room.

qa.q: What does moving downstairs mean to Dadi?
qa.a: To Dadi it means becoming "an old woman now" and leaving Dadaji's photos, which feels like losing part of herself.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows an elder resisting a small change at home, and a gentle small trial working where pushing failed.

passage:
Dear Karthik,
You asked why I'm not coming home for the long weekend. Don't panic, nothing's wrong. For two years I've taken the night bus to Kochi every single long weekend, because that's just what I do. Last month I asked myself: if there were no habit, if I were choosing fresh, what would I pick? Honestly, one weekend in Bengaluru to rest, see friends and finish my course. What stopped me was the fear that Amma would be hurt.
So I'm testing it once. I called Amma and explained. She was quiet for a second, then said, "Good, rest. We'll video call." The big hurt I was scared of didn't show up.
I'll be home for Onam, promise.
Gopika

qa.q: How has Gopika travelled home every long weekend?
qa.a: By the night bus to Kochi.

qa.q: What was Gopika afraid of before calling Amma?
qa.a: Gopika was afraid Amma would be hurt, and that fear had kept the habit going for two years.

qa.q: What two steps did Gopika take, and why do they work?
qa.a: Asking what to choose if there were no habit, then testing it once; the small test showed the feared hurt didn't appear.

qa.q: How did Amma seem to feel about the change?
qa.a: Amma seemed fine and even supportive, saying "Good, rest" and suggesting a video call.

grounding: A young adult asks what she would choose with no default and tests one small change to see whether the feared cost appears.

passage: Zainab, remember me grumbling about our daily nine o'clock meeting? Here's what I did. Everyone hated it, but nobody questioned it because it had always been there. So I asked myself: if we were starting the team from scratch, would I choose a daily meeting? No. Maybe twice a week, plus a shared notes page. But I was scared. What if people stopped talking? What if the manager thought I was lazy? So I didn't overhaul anything. I asked for a two-week test, Tuesday and Friday meetings only, and told everyone that if things slipped, we'd go back. Things didn't slip. The notes page actually got used. And Pema, the girl who hates change, now gets thanked in the corridor. Weird feeling, honestly.

qa.q: Which days did the two-week test keep meetings on?
qa.a: Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: What was Pema scared of before asking for the test?
qa.a: Pema was scared that people would stop talking or that the manager would think she was lazy.

qa.q: Why was a two-week test with a way back a wise way to question the default?
qa.a: It let the team check whether the feared problems really appeared, with a promise to go back if things slipped.

qa.q: How do Pema's colleagues seem to feel about the change?
qa.a: They seem grateful, thanking Pema in the corridor, since nobody liked the daily meeting.

grounding: A young woman asks what she would choose if there were no default meeting and runs a small reversible test of her fear.

passage: I've worked at the district library for eight years, and the hours never changed: ten to six, closed Sundays. When Farida became branch manager, she asked a strange question at her first meeting: "If we were opening this library today, with no old timings, what hours would we pick?" Somebody said evenings, because students and office workers can only come after six. The senior clerk worried nobody would come and that staff would stay late for nothing. Farida didn't argue. She said, "One month, Thursdays only, open till eight. I'll stay myself." I watched her sit at the desk that first Thursday, glancing at the door. By the fourth Thursday, forty-two people came after six. Now even Harsha from the reading room, that's me, volunteers for the late shift.

qa.q: How many people came after six by the fourth Thursday?
qa.a: Forty-two people.

qa.q: What might Farida's glances at the door on the first Thursday suggest?
qa.a: She was probably nervous that the senior clerk's fear might come true and nobody would come.

qa.q: How did Farida test the change without forcing it?
qa.a: She asked what hours they would pick with no old timings, then tried one month of Thursday evenings and stayed herself.

qa.q: How might the senior clerk see the late Thursdays after a month?
qa.a: The clerk may feel surprised and reassured, since the feared empty evenings didn't happen.

grounding: A colleague describes a new manager asking what hours they would choose with no default and testing one evening to check the feared cost.

passage: At school in Sydney, Mrs Hughes handed back the spelling tests with a sticker. "Chen, eight out of ten right! Well done." Chen grinned all the way to the bus. At home, his older brother looked at the sheet. "Two wrong? Which ones?" Chen's grin dropped. Suddenly the sticker looked silly. He went to his room and lay on the bed. "I'm bad at spelling," he told his mum at dinner. She looked at the sheet. "Eight right, two wrong. It's the same paper you were happy about at three o'clock." Chen frowned at it. It was the same paper, with the same ticks and the same two crosses. It just felt completely different.

qa.q: How many words did Chen get right?
qa.a: Eight out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Chen feel happy at school but sad at home?
qa.a: At school he heard "eight right" and felt proud; at home he heard "two wrong" and felt ashamed, even though the facts were the same.

qa.q: What could Chen's family try the next time he brings a test home?
qa.a: Say both sides, what he got right and what to practise, so one way of putting it doesn't swing his mood.

qa.q: How might Chen's brother feel if he knew his question upset Chen?
qa.a: He might feel a bit sorry, since he was only asking which words were wrong.

grounding: A boy feels proud hearing eight of ten right and sad hearing two wrong about the same spelling test.

passage: At the Saturday chess club in the community hall, Coach Tenzin handed out the puzzle sheets. "Tanvir, you solved eight of ten." Tanvir sat up straight and grinned. He was the youngest in the room. A minute later the assistant, reading results aloud for the notice board, said, "Tanvir: two puzzles missed." Tanvir's shoulders dropped. He stared at the board and didn't touch his pieces during the next game. At the break, Coach Tenzin crouched beside him. "Which one is true, eight solved or two missed?" Tanvir thought. "Both?" "Both. Same sheet. Which way helps you play the next game?" Tanvir picked up his knight. "Eight solved. And I'll practise the two."

qa.q: How many puzzles did Tanvir solve?
qa.a: Eight of ten.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's shoulders drop when the assistant read the result?
qa.a: Hearing "two puzzles missed" made him feel sad and deflated, though it was the same result that made him proud a minute earlier.

qa.q: How did Coach Tenzin help Tanvir, and why did it work?
qa.a: By asking which statement was true, the coach let Tanvir see both described the same sheet, and helped him pick a useful way to hold it.

qa.q: What would change if the assistant had read "eight solved" aloud?
qa.a: Tanvir would probably have stayed happy and played the next game with confidence.

grounding: At a chess club, a boy's mood swings from proud to sad when the same result is read as puzzles missed instead of solved.

passage:
Monday. At catching practice, Coach Anand clapped. "Sachin, eight out of ten caught! Brilliant hands." Sachin ran home and told everyone at dinner.
Wednesday. Same drill, same result, eight out of ten. This time the new assistant coach wrote on the board: "Sachin: dropped 2." Sachin read it and felt his stomach sink. On the walk home he kicked every stone. "I'm a butterfingers," he told his sister.
Friday. Before the drill, Sachin looked at Wednesday's board and then at his own notebook, where he had written Monday's "eight caught." He looked from one to the other for a long time. They were the same number, just said the other way round. That afternoon he caught nine, and he wrote it down both ways: "nine caught, one dropped."

qa.q: What did the assistant coach write on the board?
qa.a: Sachin: dropped 2.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel on Wednesday compared with Monday?
qa.a: On Monday he felt proud and excited; on Wednesday, with the same result written as dropped 2, his stomach sank and he called himself a butterfingers.

qa.q: What did Sachin do on Friday that could help him next time?
qa.a: He compared both ways of saying the result and wrote his score both ways, so one wording wouldn't control his mood.

qa.q: How might Coach Anand see the difference between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Coach Anand would probably notice that Sachin's catching was the same, and only the wording changed how he felt.

grounding: Across a week, a boy feels proud of eight catches and ashamed of two drops, until he sees they are the same result.

passage: The results board outside the coaching centre in Indore listed mock-test performance in bold red: "Hrithik Sharma - 40% incorrect." Hrithik stared at it on the pavement, among the pani-puri carts, while his friend Harsha checked his own line. "Forty percent wrong," Hrithik muttered. "I'm failing. I should just drop physics and take the easier elective." Harsha looked at him. "Bro, that's sixty percent right. Last month I got sixty and sir called it good." "It doesn't say sixty right. It says forty wrong." "Same number, turned around." Hrithik looked at the red line again, then at Harsha. His jaw loosened a little. "Say it the other way again." "Sixty percent right." Hrithik let out a breath. "Okay. Maybe not drop physics tonight."

qa.q: What did the results board say about Hrithik?
qa.a: Hrithik Sharma - 40% incorrect.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik want to drop physics on the spot?
qa.a: Reading "40% incorrect" in red made him feel like a failure, so he panicked and wanted to escape, though it also meant sixty percent right.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do before making a choice about a subject?
qa.a: Restate the result both ways, sixty right and forty wrong, and wait a day before deciding, so the wording doesn't make the choice.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the same score?
qa.a: Harsha sees it as sixty percent right, a score his teacher once called good, and tries to show Hrithik the other side.

grounding: A teenage boy nearly drops a subject after seeing his score written as 40 percent wrong rather than 60 percent right.

passage:
"I'm not going for trials again. Coach said I lost four out of ten one-on-ones. Four!"
"Jatin, sit." Gargi didi put down her laptop. "Out of ten?"
"Yes."
"So you won six."
"That's not what he said."
"But it's what happened, na?"
"...Yes."
"How many did Neeraj win? The one who got selected?"
"Seven."
"Seven versus six. And you want to quit because of how one sentence sounded."
Jatin pulled at a thread on his jersey. "When he said lost four, it felt like I was the worst one there."
"And if he'd said won six?"
"I'd be practising in the park right now."
Gargi pointed at the door. "Then go practise. You won six."

qa.q: How many one-on-ones did Neeraj win?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: Why did Jatin want to stop going for trials?
qa.a: Hearing "lost four out of ten" made him feel like the worst one there, so he felt discouraged enough to quit.

qa.q: How does Gargi didi help Jatin see the result differently?
qa.a: She restates it as winning six and compares it with Neeraj's seven, showing he was close, not the worst.

qa.q: How does Gargi didi seem to see Jatin's plan to quit?
qa.a: She sees it as an overreaction to how one sentence sounded, and pushes him to go and practise.

grounding: A teenage boy nearly quits trials after hearing he lost four of ten, until his sister restates it as winning six.

passage: Last year, the career counsellor at school ran our marks through a chart and said, "Vaibhav, there's a forty percent chance you won't make the cut-off for the design college." I heard "won't make it" and nothing else. That night I nearly withdrew my application and told Ammi I'd just take the local college. Then Hafsa, my classmate, said her counsellor had told her, "You have a sixty percent chance." Her marks were almost the same as mine. She was excited; I was crushed. Same number, flipped. I went back and asked the counsellor to say it the other way. Sixty percent. It felt like a different future. I applied. I got in, but even if I hadn't, at least the choice would have been mine, not the sentence's.

qa.q: What chance did Hafsa's counsellor give her?
qa.a: A sixty percent chance.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav almost withdraw the application?
qa.a: Vaibhav heard only "won't make it" in the forty percent wording and felt crushed and hopeless, though it matched a sixty percent chance.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that others could copy?
qa.a: Ask for the same number said the other way before making a big choice, so the wording doesn't decide.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa have felt excited with almost the same marks?
qa.a: Her counsellor put it as a sixty percent chance of success, so she heard hope rather than failure.

grounding: A teenager recalls nearly withdrawing an application because a chance was worded as failure, while a classmate heard the same odds as success.

passage: At the university's career fair, two stalls sold the same data-analytics course from rival institutes, at the same fee. The first banner said, in gold: 90% OF OUR STUDENTS GET PLACED! The second, a plain printed sheet, said: 10% of our students were not placed last year. Santosh was already at the gold banner, filling in the form. Himani read both. "Santosh, look. They say the same thing." "No, the second one sounds bad. Ten percent not placed? That's scary." "And ninety percent placed isn't?" Santosh paused, pen hovering. "When you say it like that, they're identical." "The second one is just more honest about who it leaves out," Himani said. Santosh put the pen down and asked both stalls the same question: how many students, and placed where?

qa.q: What did the second stall's sheet say?
qa.a: 10% of our students were not placed last year.

qa.q: Why was Santosh drawn to the gold banner?
qa.a: The placed wording made Santosh feel hopeful and excited, while the not-placed wording of the same figure felt scary.

qa.q: What question did Santosh finally ask, and why is it useful?
qa.a: How many students, and placed where, which turns both wordings into actual numbers that can be compared.

qa.q: How does Himani see the two stalls?
qa.a: Himani sees them as saying the same thing, with the second simply more honest about who it leaves out.

grounding: A student is drawn to a course advertised by its success rate and put off by the same figure stated as a failure rate.

passage:
Hi Salma,
A funny thing happened while I was laptop shopping, and I think you'll enjoy it. Shop A had a huge poster: "SAVE 20%! Festival offer!" I felt this rush, like I'd miss out if I didn't buy right then. Shop B, two doors down, had the same model with a small tag: "Price after festival discount: 80% of MRP." I nearly walked past. It sounded like I was paying almost full price. Then I did the maths on my phone. Exactly the same amount. Same laptop, same price, same warranty. The only difference was that one sentence made me feel like I was winning and the other made me feel like I was losing.
I bought from Shop B, just to prove to myself I could.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Shop B's tag say?
qa.a: Price after festival discount: 80% of MRP.

qa.q: How did Shop A's poster make Chaitanya feel?
qa.a: It gave Chaitanya a rush and a fear of missing out, as if buying right then meant winning.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya see through the wording?
qa.a: Doing the maths on the phone to compare the actual amounts, which showed both offers were identical.

qa.q: What would change if Shop B used Shop A's poster?
qa.a: Shop B would probably draw far more buyers, even though nothing about the laptop or the price changed.

grounding: A student writes about being pulled by a 'save 20%' poster and nearly passing up the same price worded as 80 percent.

passage: Tushar, you know that music app I've been paying for? I signed up because the pop-up said, "Just 99 rupees a month, less than a cup of coffee!" I felt so smart. It sounded tiny. Yesterday I was checking my bank app and saw the yearly total: eleven hundred and eighty-eight rupees. I actually said "what?" out loud in the library. Same thing, right? Ninety-nine times twelve. But one felt like a coffee and the other felt like a pair of shoes. And when the trial ended, the message said, "Don't lose your playlists!", which is why I didn't cancel. Losing felt worse than paying. So now I write every offer three ways: per month, per year, and what I'd lose. Anand's new hobby. Very exciting stuff.

qa.q: What yearly total did Anand see?
qa.a: Eleven hundred and eighty-eight rupees.

qa.q: How did Anand feel on seeing the yearly total?
qa.a: Anand felt shocked, saying "what?" out loud, because the same cost now felt like a pair of shoes instead of a coffee.

qa.q: What habit has Anand started, and why does it help?
qa.a: Writing every offer three ways, per month, per year and what would be lost, so no single wording decides.

qa.q: How might Tushar react to Anand's story?
qa.a: Tushar may laugh but also check Tushar's own subscriptions, seeing how a small monthly figure hides the bigger total.

grounding: A student describes how a monthly price and a 'don't lose your playlists' message steered a choice that the yearly figure would not have.

passage: At the panchayat meeting in a village near Wardha, the seed company's leaflet said the new cotton variety "reduces crop loss by 50 percent!" Everyone murmured. Madhav, the young agriculture officer, stood up with the leaflet. "Let's say it three ways before anyone decides. Fifty percent less loss sounds big. But on our fields, loss has been about four quintals out of a hundred. So this seed saves around two quintals. And the seed costs more, so some of you could still end up with less in hand if prices fall." Tarun, who farmed six acres, scratched his head. "So it's good, but not magic." "Good for some fields, magic for none," Madhav said. "I'll show my working to anyone who wants it. You decide."

qa.q: How much has loss been on their fields, according to Madhav?
qa.a: About four quintals out of a hundred.

qa.q: Why did Madhav stand up with the leaflet?
qa.a: He felt concerned that "50 percent less loss" would sound bigger than it was, and wanted the farmers to decide from fair numbers.

qa.q: How did Madhav frame the choice fairly?
qa.a: He restated it as a percentage, as actual quintals saved and as a possible downside if prices fall, then left the choice to the farmers.

qa.q: How does Tarun see the seed after Madhav speaks?
qa.a: Tarun sees it as good but not magic, a clearer picture than the leaflet gave.

grounding: A young officer restates a seed offer as gain, as loss and in plain quintals before farmers decide, rather than steering them.

passage: In the planning office in Oslo, Siddiq had two slides ready for the council. His manager's draft said, "The new crossing will cut accidents by 25 percent!" Siddiq added a line under it: "That means from about eight a year to about six." Then a second slide: "Put another way, even with the crossing we expect around six accidents a year. The cost is four months of roadworks outside the school." Astrid, a council member known for hard questions, read both slides. "Your manager's version sounded like a miracle," she said. "Yours sounds like a fair trade." "I want you to choose it for the right reasons," Siddiq said, "or turn it down for the right reasons." The council voted yes, and later nobody felt tricked.

qa.q: What does a 25 percent cut mean in accidents per year?
qa.a: From about eight a year to about six.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq add lines under his manager's slide?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about steering the council with a percentage that sounded like a miracle, and wanted them to see the real numbers and the cost.

qa.q: What makes Siddiq's slides a fair way to present a choice?
qa.a: They give the percentage, the plain numbers, what remains and the cost, so the council decides on the full picture.

qa.q: How does Astrid see Siddiq's version?
qa.a: Astrid sees it as a fair trade rather than a miracle, and seems to trust it more.

grounding: A young planner restates a benefit in plain numbers, as what remains and with its cost, so the council is not steered by one framing.

passage: The hostel committee had to choose between two mess caterers, and the notice Preeti found pinned up that morning said: "New caterer: 80% of students at St. Joseph's loved the food!" She took it down before the vote. At the meeting she wrote on the whiteboard instead: "At St. Joseph's, 80 out of 100 liked it; 20 out of 100 didn't. Our current caterer: 70 liked, 30 didn't. New one costs 300 more per month." Mridul, the mess secretary, frowned. "The old notice was more exciting." "It was written to make us vote one way," Preeti said. "I'd rather we choose knowing both sides." The vote was close. The new caterer won, and nobody complained later that they'd been sold something.

qa.q: How many out of 100 at St. Joseph's didn't like the new caterer's food?
qa.a: 20 out of 100.

qa.q: Why did Preeti take the notice down before the vote?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable with a notice written to push the vote one way, and wanted everyone to choose knowing both sides.

qa.q: How did Preeti's whiteboard make the choice fairer?
qa.a: It showed who liked and disliked each caterer in plain numbers, plus the extra cost, instead of one exciting percentage.

qa.q: How does Mridul react to Preeti's version?
qa.a: Mridul finds the old notice more exciting, but the fair version meant nobody felt sold something later.

grounding: A young woman replaces a one-sided notice with both likes and dislikes in plain numbers so others can choose fairly.

passage:
Monday. The new girl, Sharmila, was the tallest in Class 4 and laughed at everyone's jokes. By lunch Siddharth had decided she was the smartest person in the class, and the most honest too. "She's just nice," he told his mother. "You can tell."
Wednesday. In the maths group, Sharmila said the answer was 48. Siddharth had worked out 36, but he rubbed his out and wrote 48 because she sounded so sure. The teacher marked it wrong.
Friday. Siddharth saw Sharmila copy the science homework from Parth's notebook and then smile at the teacher. He stood by the water tap, confused. She was still cheerful. She was still tall. But being cheerful hadn't made her right about 48, and it didn't make copying honest. He walked back to class slowly, his head full.

qa.q: What answer had Siddharth worked out before rubbing it out?
How did Siddharth feel at the water tap on Friday?
qa.a: He felt confused and a little let down, because the glow he had given Sharmila didn't match her copying or her wrong answer.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do the next time he is unsure whose answer is right?
qa.a: Trust and check his own working, rather than choosing the answer of whoever seems nicest or surest.

qa.q: What would change if Siddharth had kept his own answer on Wednesday?
qa.a: His group would have got the maths right, and he might have seen sooner that Sharmila's cheerfulness said nothing about her maths.

grounding: Over a week, a boy assumes a tall, cheerful new classmate is smart and honest, until her wrong answer and copying show otherwise.

passage: Aadhya, you keep saying Meher must be the best at everything because she's so pretty and always smiling. Let your Rajni nani tell you about Sushila. When I was ten, Sushila was the tallest girl in our school, with two long plaits and the loudest laugh. I thought she was the smartest and most honest person alive. When the class money box went missing, the teacher asked who had been near it, and Sushila said she saw Kamla there. I believed her at once. Poor Kamla, quiet and thin, cried all afternoon. Two days later the box was found in Sushila's bag. I remember feeling so foolish. Her smile hadn't changed at all. It had just never told me anything about her honesty.

qa.q: Where was the money box found?
qa.a: In Sushila's bag, two days later.

qa.q: Why did young Rajni believe Sushila so quickly?
qa.a: She admired Sushila's height, plaits and laugh, so she felt sure Sushila was honest too, without any real evidence.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Rajni have judged more fairly?
qa.a: When Sushila blamed Kamla; she could have asked what anyone actually saw instead of trusting the girl she admired.

qa.q: What was it like for Kamla to be blamed?
qa.a: Kamla was blamed on Sushila's word and cried all afternoon, hurt and helpless.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, at ten, a tall, cheerful classmate's glow made her believe the girl was honest, and an innocent child was blamed.

passage: The project partners had to be chosen in five minutes, before the bell, and Dolma had been absent the week before, so she knew almost nobody in her new Gangtok school. She picked fast. Kishore was the tallest boy in the class, always laughing, and everybody crowded round him at break. Surely someone like that was clever and would do his share. For a week, Kishore talked brilliantly about their volcano model and did nothing. Twice he said he had forgotten the clay at home. The night before it was due, Dolma sat alone mixing baking soda by lamplight during a power cut. The next day, Kishore charmed the teacher with a joke while presenting. Dolma held the volcano and said nothing, her cheeks hot.

qa.q: What did Kishore say twice?
qa.a: That he had forgotten the clay at home.

qa.q: Why did Dolma assume Kishore would do his share?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and a little dazzled, because his height, laughter and popularity made him seem clever and reliable, though she had no real evidence.

qa.q: What could Dolma try the next time she picks a partner in a hurry?

grounding: Over a week, a teenage boy nearly trusts a gamer's money claim because he admires the gamer's skill, until his father helps him check.

passage: Kishore, you think that fitness star knows everything because he's handsome and famous? Sit. Let your Yusuf uncle tell you something. At fifteen, my hero was a film actor with perfect hair and a smile on every poster in Hyderabad. When he said on TV that a certain tonic made him strong and sharp, I spent my whole Eid money on three bottles. I drank it every morning before school and felt exactly the same, only poorer. My ammi asked the pharmacist, who laughed kindly and said, "It's mostly sugar syrup." I was so angry, not at the actor, at myself. He was a good actor. That was all he had ever shown me. After that, I asked one question about every famous face: good at what, exactly?

qa.q: What did young Yusuf spend his Eid money on?
qa.a: Three bottles of the tonic.

qa.q: Why was young Yusuf so angry at himself after the pharmacist spoke?
qa.a: He felt foolish and angry, realising he had trusted the actor about health only because he admired his looks and acting.

qa.q: What question did Yusuf start asking, and why is it useful?
qa.a: "Good at what, exactly?" It separates the skill someone really has from everything else they claim.

qa.q: How might the pharmacist have seen young Yusuf's bottles?
qa.a: The pharmacist seemed kind and a little amused, knowing the tonic was mostly sugar syrup and not wanting to embarrass the boy.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at fifteen, admiration for a handsome actor made him believe the actor's health claim about a tonic.

passage: The cooperative bank in Tumkur was hiring two trainee clerks, and Kavitha, only a year into the job herself, sat at the end of the panel taking notes. The next candidate, Gopika, was nervous and quiet, and got all five right. "Sir," Kavitha said carefully, "could we score each column one by one, for all candidates, before moving to the next?" qa.a: She might have lost the job despite getting every sum right, simply because she was quieter.

grounding: A junior on an interview panel sees a charming candidate rated excellent across the board and proposes scoring each skill separately.

passage: At the student union in Copenhagen, Emil sat beside Freja on the interview panel for the events team. qa.a: She may feel a little embarrassed but also relieved to have caught it before it decided the place.

grounding: A student on an interview panel sees a charming candidate scored high on everything and suggests rating each skill on its own evidence.

passage: In the small office behind the school library, Vinita had six appraisal forms to finish by Friday. Charu's was the hardest, because Charu was everyone's favourite: the students adored her, and her science fair had been in the newspaper. Vinita's first instinct was to tick "excellent" all the way down. Instead she took the form one row at a time, asking herself for a real example each time. Teaching: the science fair, the class results. Excellent. Communication with parents: two complaints about unanswered messages this term. Needs work. Record-keeping: attendance registers late four times. Satisfactory. When Charu read it, she was hurt for a moment. Then she said, "The parent messages, that's fair. Nobody's ever told me that."

qa.q: Why was Vinita's first instinct to tick excellent all the way down?

qa.a: Rating one row at a time with a real example for each, so Charu's strong teaching didn't lift other areas unearned.

qa.q: How did Charu react to the review?
qa.a: She was hurt for a moment, then accepted the point about parent messages, saying nobody had ever told her.

grounding: A young reviewer rates a popular teacher one trait at a time with examples, so her star teaching does not lift every score.
